bihar_raw_news.title: Bihar's flood risk is changing, not just repeating | Daily Pioneer
bihar_raw_news.content: October 03, 2026 Bihar’s flood risk is changing, not just repeating Copy Link X WhatsApp Share By Eklavya Prasad Bihar’s flood story is both familiar and evolving. While many communities face recurring inundation, erosion and infrastructure damage, changing flood patterns are pushing the geography of risk into new settlements, exposing more households to river floods, embankment breaches, flash floods and prolonged waterlogging Every year, Bihar counts its floods. Districts affected. Gram Panchayats affected. People evacuated. Relief camps, boats, damaged houses, families receiving gratuitous relief. These numbers matter; they let the state mobilise quickly. But after three consecutive years of flood figures, a harder question is becoming difficult to avoid: what does Bihar learn from one flood before the next arrives? The Disaster Management Department’s reports offer a starting point. On October 15, 2024, it recorded 28 affected districts, 979 Gram Panchayats and 52.46 lakh people. On October 15, 2025, the figures stood at 23 districts, 600 Gram Panchayats and 48 lakh people. The September 24, 2026 report shows 15 districts, 576 Gram Panchayats and 50.49 lakh people, a total likely to rise after the recent flooding along the Gandak. These are snapshots from different stages of different floods, so they do not measure severity. Yet the pattern is striking. The reported geography of impact has shifted considerably, while the number of people affected stays in a similar range. What changed because of what Bihar experienced the year before? Vulnerability in Bihar is neither wholly repetitive nor wholly new. Some embankments, settlements, roads and households face recurring exposure and accumulating loss. Elsewhere, a river shifts course, a breach redirects water, or a flash flood reaches people never considered at high risk. A single breach is an event; repeated breaches near the same spot signal persistent vulnerability, demanding a different response from a newly affected area. And when a flood behaves unexpectedly, that should reshape the state’s understanding of risk. Every flood produces information. Breaches are reported, roads cut, crops lost. Engineers inspect embankments; communities know where water entered and where it stagnated. When the water recedes, what happens to all this knowledge? Does a repeatedly flooded location acquire a risk profile? Does a newly affected area prompt a revision of vulnerability maps? Does a known breach or drainage failure shape how infrastructure is designed and maintained before the next monsoon? Bihar’s machinery for emergency response is extensive. What is harder to see is a learning loop connecting one year’s experience to the next year’s decisions. A response system asks: what must we do now? A learning system asks: why did this happen here, what did we learn, what must change, and who will make sure it does before it happens again? The first is indispensable during a flood. The second decides whether the state can move from recurring emergency management towards sustained risk reduction. Once the emergency passes, the questions should change. Why did the breach occur? national_raw_news.content: Prime Minister Narendra Modi today spoke with Captain Smit Machchhar over the phone, praising his bravery and presence of mind in foiling an alleged attempt to crash an Israel-bound flydubai flight. The Prime Minister said, Indians are not those who take lives, but those who are willing to risk their own lives to save others. He lauded Captain Machchhar for taking a split-second decision that helped save the lives of hundreds of passengers. On Wednesday, Captain Machchhar got seriously injured after being stabbed by his co-pilot in the cockpit of Flydubai flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The flight was carrying 174 passengers, including 27 children. The pilot is currently undergoing treatment at a hospital in the UAE. Speaking to the Prime Minister from his hospital bed, Captain Machchhar said his 17 years of flying experience, including 11 years as a captain, helped him understand the gravity of the situation and act immediately. He told the Prime Minister that he is away from the country but not from its culture. Prime Minister Modi said, special prayers were being offered across India for the pilot’s speedy recovery and thanked the governments of Saudi Arabia and the UAE for ensuring his treatment. The Prime Minister also said Captain Machchhar had enhanced the prestige of the Indian piloting community. Referring to Gandhi Jayanti being observed today, Mr Modi said the pilot had shown the world the true meaning of Ahimsa (non-violence). Captain Machchhar, who hails from Gujarat, expressed gratitude to the Prime Minister for the call and said he was receiving the best possible treatment. Mr Modi also spoke to him briefly in Gujarati.
